A_target.statement:
Let $\circ \in \set {+, -, \times, \div}$ and let $X, Y$ be [[Definition:Closed Real Interval|closed real intervals]].
Define:
:$X \circ Y = \set {x \circ y: x \in X, y \in Y}$
Then if $x \in X$ and $y \in Y$, $x \circ y \in X \circ Y$, and this enclosure property is preserved under composition of operations.

B_source.statement: $\struct {\R, +, \times}$ is a [[Definition:Field (Abstract Algebra)|field]], satisfying the [[Definition:Field Axioms|field axioms]] including existence of [[Definition:Additive Inverse|additive]] and [[Definition:Multiplicative Inverse|multiplicative inverses]].

substitutions.a real number: an interval known to contain it
substitutions.a real operation: the operation applied to the set, taking the image of the pair of intervals
substitutions.the exact real result: an interval guaranteed to enclose it

derived.the enclosure property: the computed interval always contains the true result
derived.the field identities: only partially transferred, since intervals have no additive inverses

validity_conditions: Each operation is defined as the image of the corresponding real operation on the pair of intervals, which makes the enclosure property automatic and preserved under composition.
Additive inverses fail: subtracting an interval from itself gives an interval containing zero but not equal to it, so cancellation identities do not transfer.

This is the dependency problem: an expression in which a variable occurs several times is evaluated as though the occurrences were independent, so enclosures are correct but can be far wider than necessary.
proof_plan: Replace each real quantity $x$ by a [[Definition:Closed Real Interval|closed interval]] $X \ni x$.

Define each operation as the [[Definition:Image of Subset under Mapping|image]] of the real operation on $X \times Y$.
For example:
:$\closedint a b + \closedint c d = \closedint {a + c} {b + d}$
:$\closedint a b \times \closedint c d = \closedint {\min S} {\max S}$ where $S = \set {a c, a d, b c, b d}$

If $x \in X$ and $y \in Y$ then $x \circ y \in X \circ Y$ by definition.
By [[Principle of Mathematical Induction|induction]] on the expression, any composite of operations encloses the true real result.

Identities relying on cancellation fail.
For example, with $X = \closedint 0 1$:
:$X - X = \closedint {-1} 1 \ne \set 0$
and [[Definition:Distributive Operation|distributivity]] weakens to subdistributivity $X \paren {Y + Z} \subseteq X Y + X Z$.
{{qed}}
